children: By Mark R. Long
U.S. railroads continued to benefit from shippers shifting cargo to rail from trucks, with Union Pacific, Norfolk Southern and CSX this week posting higher quarterly revenues and profits.

Soaring diesel prices and tight trucking capacity stemming in part from a crackdown on immigrant drivers have spurred demand for more-efficient rail. It is around three to four times more fuel-efficient to ship goods by rail than in a truck on a highway. Intermodal containers and trailers transported by railroads increased 12.6% from a year earlier in the week ended Oct. 17, according to the Association of American Railroads.

CSX, (Union Pacific) and (Norfolk Southern) reported volume increases of 5%, 6% and 3%, respectively, in the third quarter. The companies benefited from fuel surcharges, though fuel expenses weighed on margins.

Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena said his company and Norfolk Southern continue to work toward closing a $71.5 billion deal to combine their networks, which is expected to close in mid-2027. The merger has faced resistance from federal regulators, customers and rivals who argue it would drive up freight prices and reduce competition. The companies sent supplemental information to regulators in July, adding commitments to ensure the proposed deal would provide faster, more reliable service as promised.
U.S. railroads are planning to raise rates for intermodal shipping in coming contract renewals with shippers. (Journal of Commerce)

Commodities
U.S. Steel plans to invest nearly $3 billion in a new hot strip mill at its plant near Pittsburgh, the Journal's Kelly Cloonan writes.

U.S. Steel, which is owned by Tokyo's Nippon Steel, said the investment will replace aging equipment with modern steelmaking technology, increasing annual production capacity to about 3.5 million tons from 2.2 million tons. The move also aims to expand the range of steels that U.S. Steel can produce.

A hot strip mill makes steel slabs into thin coils used to manufacture products including vehicles, appliances and construction materials. With the investment, the company expects to better compete across the automotive, appliance and line pipe markets. U.S. Steel said it expects initial production at the mill in late 2029.
China's rising aluminum production and exports are offsetting war-related supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf, keeping global prices in check. (WSJ)
Number of the Day
Panama Canal transits in the 12 months ending Sept. 30, up 4.1% from the previous fiscal year, with growth driven by strong energy and containership activity, according to the Panama Canal Authority
Aviation

Deadly global conflicts have disrupted civil aviation, leaving fewer, longer options for safe journeys-particularly between Europe and Asia. The Houthi strikes on Saudi airports over the past month upended one of the few remaining routes used by airlines, tracking data from Flightradar24 show.

The WSJ's Benjamin Katz, Daniel Kiss and Jason French write that, outside of rare, complete airspace closures or foreign bans, airlines are left to make their own decisions on where to fly based on regulator warnings and input from private security agencies.

FedEx is among the cargo carriers that have added hours to flights to get to places such as Dubai. The freight giant's new route-which flies closer to China to minimize time in both Afghan and Pakistani airspace-adds an extra five hours.
American Airlines said it was on course for an adjusted loss in the current quarter, as surging fuel prices more than offset continued revenue strength. (WSJ)
United Airlines carried over 159,660 tons of cargo in the third quarter, a record for that period. (Air Cargo News)
In Other News
Mortgage rates fell for the first time in nine weeks, with the 30-year fixed rate averaging 7.32% this week, according to Freddie Mac. (WSJ)
Canada's industrial-product-price index rose 2% in September from the month before and jumped 14.5% compared with a year earlier. (WSJ)
S&P Global flash purchasing managers indexes showed diverging private-sector business activity in India, Australia and Japan in October. (WSJ)
Japan's consumer prices excluding fresh food rose 2.1% in September from a year earlier, up from a 1.7% increase in August. (WSJ)
Consumer sentiment in the U.K. tumbled at the fastest pace since the Covid-19 pandemic this month. (WSJ)
Saudi Aramco is working to increase the capacity of its East-West oil pipeline to 10 million barrels a day, CEO Amin Nasser said. (WSJ)
Volvo Car said it would cut an additional 2,500 jobs, or around 6% of its workforce, as it targets $500 million in cost savings. (WSJ)

Honeywell Technologies raised its full-year outlook following its first quarter as a stand-alone company, saying gains in building and process automation and technology offset a drop in industrial automation. (WSJ)
The Trump administration pledged to buy Lockheed Martin F-35 jet fighters for the next decade in a framework agreement covering 850 aircraft. (WSJ)
Westinghouse Electric plans to invest $1 billion in a new nuclear-fuel factory next to an existing South Carolina plant. (South Carolina Daily Gazette)
President Trump said he would postpone tariffs on wind turbines and parts and have officials consult with trading partners and report back in 180 days. (Bloomberg)
The U.S. and Denmark signed an agreement aimed at supporting the American shipbuilding workforce, attracting Danish shipyard investment and speeding vessel construction. (Reuters)
